method: Controller's direct review of the complete captions and editor-supplied matching transcript, using the editor's independent identification of the opening speaker, explicit naming, book ownership, and local question-answer continuity.
confidenceScope: Identity of the speaker advancing each selected proposition and its eligible quotation, not word-level diarization of every rolling caption or confidence in every ASR word. All material-wording confidence fields remain unchanged. An inherited generic no-audio rationale is not itself evidence of ambiguous identity; each proposition is reviewed on its actual text.
limitations: The user transcript reproduces the same caption words, so it is not a second independent transcription.
Rolling caption boundaries can retain a preceding word, a following word, or a short interlocutor interjection. Those words must not be treated as the selected speaker's proposition.
No claims about tone, emphasis, vocal confidence, or inaudible words may enter scoring. Garbled incidental words cannot justify a participant penalty.
If either isolated judge identifies a genuinely material unresolved wording or attribution problem, stop before adjudication; this review cannot waive such a problem.

moves.rationale: This is the uninterrupted substantive opening identified by the editor as Sam. His revised football analogy leads directly to the doctrine examples; Haidt then answers by granting that specific doctrines matter.
The answering speaker grants Sam's preceding thought experiment and asks him to specify his analogy's end zone. The second-person request and Sam's immediate answer establish Haidt as the questioner.

Sam answers Haidt's end-zone question with paradise and avoidance of hell, then later explicitly narrows his answer to ISIS. The inherited rationale naming Haidt was a copied annotation error; the speaker field, proposition and answer sequence identify Harris.

After Sam's paradise answer, the interlocutor contrasts his own resistance to parsimony and names social bonding as closer to his account. Sam then replies that he meant ISIS specifically. This bracketed objection is Haidt's.

The speaker corrects the scope of his own end-zone claim, distinguishing ISIS from Unitarians and religious people generally. It answers Haidt's multiple-goals objection and resumes the editor-identified opening argument.

The turn grants Sam's point, then addresses his two religion books and criticizes their focus on explicit explanations. This is Haidt replying to the immediately preceding ISIS clarification, not Sam criticizing his own books.

The speaker answers the criticism of his books with fundamentalists' self-understanding and addresses the other speaker's moral foundations theory. Haidt then explicitly agrees and proposes distinguishing fundamentalism from religion generally. The initial rolling tail is not part of Harris's claim.

The speaker contrasts his own adaptation view with Dawkins and the addressee, then explicitly denies deriving present moral goodness directly from evolution. Sam subsequently probes a naturalistic inference and Haidt rejects it, citing Sam's Moral Landscape in the second person.

Following Haidt's denial of a naturalistic inference, Sam distinguishes descriptive history from moral possibility and challenges a tacit assumption about religious goods. Haidt replies that it is a fine point and he agrees. The quoted no-better-way assumption is the target of Sam's criticism, not Sam's endorsed conclusion.

Haidt's response begins by agreeing with Sam and develops the contrast between nested groups and erased boundaries. The continuous institutional proposal is followed by Sam's first-person reply about his secularism books; Haidt then addresses that speaker by name as Sam.

The speaker responds to the nested-institution proposal, names his own secularism books, and argues for secular rational construction. The immediately following response explicitly says totally agree sam. The initial rolling word disaster belongs to the preceding turn, not this proposition.

Sam introduces the next topic by summarizing the other speaker's research and asking whether he has summarized it accurately. The answer limits skepticism to individual reason and explains institutional correction; the same research-owning speaker then introduces his moral-dumbfounding experiments.

The speaker gives a continuous first-person account of his graduate and university research and experiments, following Sam's request to introduce moral dumbfounding. Sam then asks what he takes that evidence to imply. The experimental report is Haidt's.

Sam interrupts the research report with a second-person question about an implication he thinks Haidt draws, explicitly inviting correction. Haidt immediately denies the implication. The fragment about there being no truth belongs to Sam's question, not an endorsed denial of moral truth.

The speaker explicitly denies ever making the inference Sam has just attributed to him and separates his research from his philosophical disagreement. He proceeds to propose anthropocentric truth, later identifying his addressee as Sam during that exposition.

The speaker explicitly says my book the moral landscape while explaining plural peaks and misery-filled valleys. Haidt's brief agreement with the metaphor is an interjection, not ownership of the main argument.

The speaker recounts how Wiggins influenced him, addresses The Moral Landscape as the other speaker's book, and directly says Sam during his gold/silver comparison. This identifies Haidt independently of the general position being defended.

The same anthropocentric-facts speaker moves from markets to women's political rights and ends by asking the interlocutor whether equality is like conductivity. Sam answers with his possible-minds framework. The rights challenge is Haidt's continuous exposition.

Sam answers Haidt's conductivity question by disputing the anthropocentric boundary and specifying the position already tied to his book. Haidt briefly grants the other-things-equal suffering comparison; that concession does not transfer authorship of Sam's larger reply.

Sam's possible-minds answer continues into what the moral landscape allows concerning alternative gender arrangements, before his condemnation of present oppression. Haidt enters with a war-context observation and a new second-person question; the selected equality argument precedes that turn.

After agreeing that the described societies are horrific, Haidt asks whether the research program in The Moral Landscape can determine alien morality. The second-person challenge addresses Sam's named framework and elicits Sam's answer.

Haidt restates his question about whether evolutionary history is essential; Sam answers with the newly created conscious computer. Haidt immediately grants suffering as one dimension and asks about rights, separating the two speakers' propositions clearly.

The reply grants Sam's suffering example, addresses rights as something Sam does not discuss much in The Moral Landscape, and develops the clonal-species comparison. Sam then answers by distinguishing descriptive and normative projects.

Sam's direct answer to the clonal-species challenge grants what evolutionary history predicts and calls morality a subset of well-being. Haidt interrupts by calling this your definition, which confirms the attribution of the preceding definition to Sam.

Sam resumes after Haidt's definition objection, says he may not have fully answered the question, and argues for leaving tribal violence behind. Haidt then again calls this your conception, distinguishing his response from Sam's argument.

Following Sam's little-girl comparison, Haidt grants greater flourishing other things equal but challenges experiential addition, referring to his previous replies to Sam and his classroom exercise. Sam responds with his own Kahneman conversation.

Sam answers Haidt's classroom example with his private conversation with Kahneman and the experienced/remembered distinction. Haidt interrupts that he means something even beyond that; the remembered-self exposition belongs to Sam's reply.

This concise interruption explicitly goes beyond the remembered-self answer and restates the meaning, purpose and accomplishment objection. Sam immediately responds that all of that can be bundled into the remembered self, identifying the intervening objection as Haidt's.

Sam answers the beyond-happiness objection by including meaning, connections and ordeals within well-being. Haidt then requests a topic change because of office hours; Sam agrees to table the issue. The final area-under-the-curve defense is Sam's, not the topic-changing guest's.

publicationRequirements: Disclose caption-based assessment and editor-confirmed opening speaker, with no audio verification.
Preserve Haidt's concessions that doctrine matters and greater flourishing is better other things equal; do not present him as denying moral truth or all reason.
Present Harris's European-demography passage as his historical hypothetical, not an independently verified current fact.
Introduce quotations from challenged assumptions or diagnostic questions with enough context to prevent reversing the speaker's position.
